content.body: Finding the middle of a list sounds simple, but what if you can't count the items first? In linked lists, you can only walk node by node. Let's learn how to find the middle efficiently with just one pass.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply the two-pointer technique to traverse a linked list
• Implement a function that returns the middle node
• Explain why we can't use direct indexing in linked lists
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have a chain of 5 connected boxes (nodes). Each box only knows about the next box in line. How would you find the middle box if you can only look at one box at a time, starting from the first?
content.title: Try it
content.visualMetaphor: Show node-to-node traversal; one step at a time along the chain.

content.body: You probably walked through the chain, counting as you went. That's natural! But with linked lists, we need to be careful: we can't jump back to the beginning once we reach the end.
content.title: What you did

content.body: What if the list has 1000 nodes? Walking through twice (once to count, once to find middle) is inefficient. We need a way to find the middle in a single pass. Can't figure it out? The next step will show you.
content.title: Why it gets tricky

content.body: Add a pointer mental model first: we can only move to next (or prev); we cannot jump by index. In linked lists, we walk node by node with pointers. To find the middle efficiently, we'll use two pointers moving at different speeds.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of two people walking along the same chain: one takes two steps for every one step the other takes. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one will be at the middle.

content.body: We'll use two pointers: 'slow' moves one node at a time, 'fast' moves two nodes at a time. When 'fast' reaches the end, 'slow' will be at the middle. This works for both odd and even lengths!
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start both pointers at the head of the list
2. While fast pointer and fast.next exist:
   • Move slow one step forward
   • Move fast two steps forward
3. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle
4. Return the slow pointer
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called middleNode that takes a linked list head as parameter.
steps.hint: Remember: head is the first node in the list.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure you name it middleNode and accept a head parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function called middleNode(head).

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create two pointers: slow and fast, both starting at the head.
steps.hint: Set both variables equal to head initially.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Both pointers are ready to start walking.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Make sure you create both slow and fast variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need slow = head and fast = head.

steps.title: Traverse with the two-pointer technique
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as fast exists AND fast.next exists. Inside, move slow one step and fast two steps.
steps.hint: Use while(fast && fast.next) and update pointers: slow = slow.next, fast = fast.next.next
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The pointers are now moving at different speeds.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Check that your loop condition and pointer updates are correct.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: while(fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }

steps.title: Return the middle node
steps.instruction: After the loop ends, return the slow pointer (which now points to the middle node).
steps.hint: Simply return slow after the while loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the complete solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Make sure you're returning the correct pointer.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: when the loop ends, slow is at the middle. Return it!

content.body: Great work! You've learned how to find the middle of a linked list using the two-pointer technique. Remember: in linked lists, we walk node by node—no direct indexing allowed. The fast-slow pointer approach lets us find the middle in one pass, which is efficient and elegant!
